# Improving without overfitting {#sec-improvements}

```{python}
exec(open("_common.py").read())
import json
r2 = json.loads((ROOT / "models" / "round2_experiments.json").read_text())
r3 = json.loads((ROOT / "models" / "round3_recency.json").read_text())
```

The report card (@sec-reportcard) showed where the model trails the market. The
temptation is to keep trying ideas until one "works". That's how models overfit: with
enough tries, something always looks good by luck. So every improvement here follows one
rule, written down **before** running anything.

::: {.callout-important}
## The anti-overfitting rule
1. Pre-register a short list of candidates. No trying things until something sticks.
2. Decide on the **2021–2023** out-of-sample seasons only. Adopt a candidate only if its
   margin error beats the current model in **at least 2 of those 3 seasons** and the
   paired bootstrap 95% interval of the improvement **excludes zero**.
3. Use **2024–2025** only as a check, never to choose.
4. Log every attempt, including failures, in `docs/experiments/`.
5. The live 2026 season is the real test.
:::

## Preseason information (adopted)

The biggest gap was the first weeks of the season: the model knew last year's team, not
this year's. Four families of information known **before week 1** were added:

| Feature | Source | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| Transfer portal in/out and net stars | CFBD `/player/portal` (2021+) | Roster turnover |
| Recruiting class points, 4-year average | CFBD `/recruiting/teams` | Talent pipeline |
| New head coach | CFBD `/coaches` (hire dates) | Coach who starts the season hired in the last 12 months |
| Preseason AP poll points | CFBD `/rankings`, week 1 | Expert consensus in August |

: Preseason features. Portal entries dated after the season started: at most 0.2%. {#tbl-preseason}

| Margin error gap vs the closing line (points) | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 2021–23, weeks 0–2 (decision) | 1.96 | **1.84** |
| 2021–23, whole season (decision) | 0.63 | **0.59** |
| 2024–25, weeks 0–2 (check) | 1.32 | **1.11** |
| 2024–25, whole season (check) | 0.60 | **0.57** |

: Random forest, before vs after the preseason features (from `docs/experiments/2026-09-23_preseason_features.md`). {#tbl-preseason-gain}

The gap narrows where it was aimed and holds in the check seasons, so the family was
adopted. It doesn't close: early in the season the market still knows about quarterback
battles, injuries and depth charts.

## Round 2: a more robust model (nothing adopted)

```{python}
#| label: tbl-round2
#| tbl-cap: "Round 2 candidates. Decision seasons 2021–2023; check seasons 2024–2025."
t2 = pd.DataFrame(r2["table"])
v2 = pd.DataFrame(r2["verdicts"]).T
dec = t2[t2.period == "decide 2021-23"].set_index("candidate")
chk = t2[t2.period == "check 2024-25"].set_index("candidate")
out = pd.DataFrame({
    "Margin 21–23": dec["margin MAE"], "Total 21–23": dec["total MAE"],
    "O/U 21–23": dec["O/U open %"], "Margin 24–25": chk["margin MAE"],
    "O/U 24–25": chk["O/U open %"],
}).round(2)
out.index.name = None
out
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-round2-verdict
#| tbl-cap: "Round 2 verdicts under the rule (margin error, decision seasons 2021–2023)."
vv = v2.rename(columns={"seasons better than A (of 3)": "Seasons better (of 3)",
                        "margin MAE gain 95% CI": "Gain, 95% interval", "adopt": "Adopted"})
vv.index.name = None
vv.drop(index="A current (RF)")
```

Averaging the six tuned models (B) was best in both periods, but its interval touches
zero, so under the rule it isn't adopted. It now runs every week as a **shadow model**
(stored, not used for picks) so the 2026 season can settle it. Dedicated margin/total
models and clipping blowouts in training were worse.

## Round 3: making recent information count more (nothing adopted)

```{python}
#| label: tbl-round3
#| tbl-cap: "Round 3 candidates: season recency weights (R1), 30-day form ratings with momentum (R2), both (R3)."
t3 = pd.DataFrame(r3["table"])
v3 = pd.DataFrame(r3["verdicts"]).T
d3 = t3[t3.period == "decide 2021-23"].set_index("candidate")[["margin MAE", "O/U open %"]]
c3 = t3[t3.period == "check 2024-25"].set_index("candidate")[["margin MAE", "O/U open %"]]
out3 = pd.DataFrame({
    "Margin 21–23": d3["margin MAE"], "O/U 21–23": d3["O/U open %"],
    "Margin 24–25": c3["margin MAE"], "O/U 24–25": c3["O/U open %"],
}).round(2)
out3.index.name = None
out3
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-round3-verdict
#| tbl-cap: "Round 3 verdicts under the rule (margin error, decision seasons 2021–2023)."
vv3 = v3.rename(columns={"seasons better (of 3)": "Seasons better (of 3)",
                         "gain 95% CI": "Gain, 95% interval", "adopt": "Adopted"})
vv3.index.name = None
vv3.drop(index="A current")
```

This is what overfitting looks like when you catch it. R1 and R2 look good on the
2024–25 totals (around 52%) but are **worse** on 2021–23 (around 50%). An effect that
flips between periods is noise. Choosing from 2024–25 alone would have "improved" the
model on paper and hurt it in reality.

Recent information already counts at its tuned optimum: the ratings' 120-day half-life
beat a 60-day one (@tbl-ridge-grid), and last-3-games and residual-form features already
exist. With about 12 games per team, short-term form mostly regresses to the mean.

## Conclusion

The remaining gap to the market is **information, not modeling**. What the books know
and the model doesn't: the starting quarterback and injuries, the weather for totals,
and bowl opt-outs. Those are the next data sources (@sec-roadmap).
